Story · Lesson 1

The Longest Line

Omar has been standing in a line since six in the morning. Read the story, then read Omar's story the next day.

Say how long something has been happeningDescribe what people have been doingCompare it with a finished action

1The story

It is eleven o'clock in the morning, and Omar is standing in a very long line outside a government office. He needs a new ID card, because his old one has been in the washing machine! He has been waiting here since six o'clock this morning. That's five hours.

The sun has been shining all morning, and everyone is hot and tired. The old man in front of Omar has been reading the same newspaper for two hours. Two women behind him have been talking about weddings since seven. A boy has been selling cold water up and down the line, and he has been making a lot of money.

Omar calls Adam. "What have you been doing all morning?" Adam asks. "Standing," says Omar. "Just standing. My legs hurt. I have been standing here so long that I know everyone's life story!" Adam laughs. "Are you sure you're in the right line?" "Of course I'm sure. It's the longest line here, so it's the right one."

At twelve o'clock, Omar finally reaches the window. The clerk looks at him. "ID cards? No, this line is for passports. ID cards are inside, in room three. There's no line there." Omar's mouth falls open. He walks inside. Room three is empty, and in five minutes he has a new ID card. When he comes out, the old man is still reading his newspaper. "Where have you been?" he asks. Omar smiles. "Learning a lesson!"

2Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

1
Where is Omar standing?In a long line outside a government office.
2
Why does he need a new ID card?His old one has been in the washing machine.
3
How long has he been waiting?Since six o'clock. Five hours.
4
What has the old man been doing?Reading the same newspaper for two hours.
5
What have the two women been talking about?Weddings.
6
What has the boy been selling?Cold water.
7
Has the boy been making money?Yes, a lot.
8
What has Omar been doing all morning?Standing.
9
Why does Omar think he is in the right line?Because it's the longest line.
10
What is the line for?Passports.
11
Where are the ID cards?Inside, in room three.
12
How long does it take to get the new card?Five minutes.

3Point of view Now Omar tells it the next day, when it is finished.

O

Yesterday, I waited in a very long line outside a government office. I needed a new ID card, because my old one had been in the washing machine! I stood there from six o'clock until twelve.

The sun shone all morning. The old man in front of me read the same newspaper for two hours, and the women behind me talked about weddings all morning. A boy sold cold water and made a lot of money.

At twelve, I finally reached the window. That line was for passports! The ID cards were inside, in room three, and there was no line at all. In five minutes, I had my new card.

So what did I learn? The longest line is not always the right one. Now, when people tell me, "I have been waiting for hours," I ask them, "Are you in the right line?"

4What did you learn?

You learned the present perfect continuous.

We use it for an action that started in the past and is still happening now, often to say how long.

Still happening nowFinished: past simple
He has been waiting since six.He waited for five hours.
The sun has been shining all morning.The sun shone all morning.
They have been talking for hours.They talked for hours.
What have you been doing?What did you do?
have / has + been + -ingI have been waiting. She has been reading.
for a length, since a startfor five hours · since six o'clock
Some verbs don't take -ingknow, like, want: I have known him for years.
QuestionsHow long have you been studying English?I've been studying it for three years.

5New words

linepeople waiting one behind another
governmentthe people who run a country
washing machinea machine that washes clothes
newspapernews printed on paper
reachesgets to
passportsthe small books you need to travel to other countries

Topic · Lesson 2

Helping Others

Sara has been volunteering at a children's hospital. Why do so many young people volunteer?

Talk about volunteeringSay how long you have been doing somethingGive reasons

1Read

For the last three months, Sara has been volunteering at a children's hospital in Khartoum every Friday morning. She isn't a doctor or a nurse. She reads stories, plays games, and helps the children with their homework.

A volunteer is someone who gives their time to help others without pay. Many young Sudanese people have been volunteering in recent years. They clean streets, teach children to read, give out food in Ramadan, and help families after floods.

Why do people volunteer? Some want to give back to their community. Others want to learn new skills or meet new people. And many say it simply makes them happy. "I've been feeling much better since I started," Sara says. "When a sick child laughs, it's the best feeling in the world."

Volunteering can also help your future. Employers often like to see it on a résumé, because it shows that you are responsible and good at working in a team. You don't need a lot of time. One hour a week can change someone's day. What have you been doing to help others?

2Ways to help

teachhelp children read
share foodin Ramadan
after floodshelp families clean and rebuild
hospitalsread and play with sick children

3Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

1
How long has Sara been volunteering?For three months.
2
What does she do at the hospital?She reads stories, plays games, and helps the children with their homework.
3
What is a volunteer?Someone who gives their time to help others without pay.
4
What have young Sudanese people been doing?Cleaning streets, teaching children, giving out food, and helping after floods.
5
Why do employers like to see volunteering on a résumé?It shows that you are responsible and good at working in a team.
6
How much time do you need?One hour a week can change someone's day.

At the Doctor's

Describing how you feel and for how long

Describe symptomsSay how long you have felt like thisUnderstand the doctor's advice

1Read the conversation

Adam hasn't been feeling well. He visits a doctor at the health center.
DRDOCTORGood morning, Adam. What seems to be the problem?
AADAMI've been feeling tired, and I have a sore throat.
DRDOCTORHow long have you been feeling like this?
AADAMFor about four days. And I've been coughing a lot at night.
DRDOCTORHave you had a fever?
AADAMYes, a little. Since Tuesday.
DRDOCTORLet me look at your throat. Hmm, it's red. Have you been drinking enough water?
AADAMNot really. I've been studying a lot for my exams.
DRDOCTORIt's a throat infection. Take this medicine three times a day, drink a lot of water, and rest for a few days.
AADAMThank you, Doctor. I'll take a break from studying.

Say how long

Describe it

I've been coughing a lot at night.

Answer

Have you had a fever?
— Yes, a little.

Understand advice

Take this medicine three times a day.

Story · Lesson 4

If I Were the Teacher

Hamza doesn't like homework, so he imagines a different school. Read the story, then read it from Hamza's point of view.

Imagine a different situationUse if and wouldTalk about what you would change

1The story

Hamza is eight years old, and he doesn't like school very much. One evening, he is sitting at the kitchen table with his homework. He has been looking at the same math problem for twenty minutes. "If I were the teacher," he says, "there wouldn't be any homework."

Adam smiles. "Really? What else would you change?" Hamza thinks. "If I were the teacher, school would start at ten o'clock, not seven. We would play football every morning. And if a student got a bad grade, I would give him a cookie to feel better."

"And if the students didn't listen?" Adam asks. "I would never shout," says Hamza. "I would tell them a funny story, and they would listen." "What would you do if the principal came to your class?" "If the principal came, I would ask him to play football with us!"

Their mother is listening at the door. "That sounds like a wonderful school, Hamza," she says. "But if you were the teacher, you would need to know the answer to that math problem." Hamza looks at his homework. Then he looks at Adam. "Adam, if you helped me, I would finish faster." Adam laughs. "And if I helped you every night, you would never learn!" But he sits down and helps him anyway.

2Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

1
How old is Hamza?Eight.
2
Does he like school?Not very much.
3
How long has he been looking at the math problem?For twenty minutes.
4
What wouldn't there be if Hamza were the teacher?Any homework.
5
What time would school start?At ten o'clock.
6
What would they do every morning?Play football.
7
What would he give a student who got a bad grade?A cookie.
8
Would he shout if the students didn't listen?No, he wouldn't. He would tell them a funny story.
9
What would he ask the principal?To play football with them.
10
Who is listening at the door?Their mother.
11
What would Hamza need to know if he were the teacher?The answer to the math problem.
12
Does Adam help him in the end?Yes, he does.

3Point of view Now Hamza tells it.

HA

I'm eight, and I don't like homework. Tonight, I've been looking at the same math problem for twenty minutes. If I were the teacher, there wouldn't be any homework!

If I were the teacher, school would start at ten o'clock, and we would play football every morning. If a student got a bad grade, I would give him a cookie.

I would never shout. If the students didn't listen, I would tell them a funny story. And if the principal came to my class, I would ask him to play football with us!

Mom says that if I were the teacher, I would need to know the answer to my math problem. OK, maybe she's right. But if I were Adam, I would help my little brother every night!

4What did you learn?

You learned the second conditional.

We use it for situations that are not real now, or not likely. We imagine them.

If + pastwould + verb
If I were the teacher,there wouldn't be any homework.
If a student got a bad grade,I would give him a cookie.
If the principal came,I would ask him to play.
If you helped me,I would finish faster.
Not real: the past after ifIf I were the teacher (but I'm not).
were for everyoneIf I were, if he were, if she were.
First or second?Possible: If I study, I'll pass. Imagined: If I were the teacher, I'd…
QuestionsWhat would you do if you were the teacher?If I were the teacher, I'd tell funny stories.

5New words

maththe study of numbers
gradea number or letter that shows how good your work is
shoutspeak very loudly
principalthe head of a school
wonderfulvery, very good
anywayeven so

Dream Jobs

Four students answer one question. If you could choose any job, what would it be?

Talk about dream jobsImagine with if and wouldGive reasons for your choice

1Read

We asked four students at Future Vision Institute one question. "If you could choose any job in the world, what would it be?" Here are their answers.

Adam, 20: "I would be a pilot, of course! If I flew for an airline, I would see a new city every week. And I would fly my grandfather to Port Sudan for free."

Huda, 19: "If I could choose, I would be a teacher, like Mr. Ali. I would teach in the village where my mother grew up, because there aren't enough teachers there."

Omar, 21: "I'm already a manager, but if I had more money, I would open my own company. It would repair phones and computers in every city in Sudan."

Sara, 19: "I would be an engineer who builds bridges. If Sudan had more bridges, people wouldn't wait for hours to cross the Nile."

What about you? If you had the chance, what would you do, and what would you need to learn to get there? The first step is often closer than you think.

3
Where would Huda teach?In the village where her mother grew up.
4
What would Omar do if he had more money?Open his own company.
5
What would Sara build?Bridges.
6
Why does Sudan need more bridges, says Sara?So people wouldn't wait for hours to cross the Nile.

If I Were You…

Asking for and giving advice about a big decision

Ask for adviceGive advice with If I were youTalk about possible results

1Read the conversation

Omar has a big decision to make. He talks to Adam in the café.
OOMARAdam, I need some advice. The university has offered me a place in computer science.
AADAMThat's great news! So what's the problem?
OOMARIf I went to university, I would have to stop working at the shop. And I need the money.
AADAMHmm. Can you study part-time?
OOMARMaybe. But if I did that, it would take six years, not four.
AADAMIf I were you, I'd talk to Mr. Kamal first. He may let you work fewer hours.
OOMARThat's a good idea. What would you do if he said no?
AADAMI'd still go to university. A degree would help you open your own company one day.
OOMARYou're right. I'll talk to him tomorrow.
AADAMGood luck! And if you need help with math, call Sara, not me!

2Useful phrases

Give advice

Agree

You're right.

Good luck!

Story · Lesson 7

What Did Mr. Ali Say?

A message about a test travels from student to student, and it changes on the way. Read the story, then read the exact words people said.

Report what people saidUse said and toldPass on a message correctly

1The story

On Wednesday, Mr. Ali was sick, so a new teacher, Ms. Nadia, came to class instead. At the end of the lesson, she gave the students a message from Mr. Ali. She said that there would be a short test on Sunday. She said that it would be about the stories from Units 1 and 2, and she told the students to bring a pencil.

After class, Adam called Omar, who had been absent that day. "Ms. Nadia said that the test was on Sunday," he said. "She told us that it was about Units 1 and 2." Then Omar called Huda. "Adam said that the test was on Sunday, about Unit 2."

Huda sent a message to the class group. "Omar says there's a test on Sunday about Unit 2, or maybe Monday?" Then someone wrote, "I heard that there was no test!" By Saturday night, nobody knew what was true. Some students said that the test had been canceled. Others said that it was on Monday.

On Sunday morning, Mr. Ali came back. Half of the students had pencils, and the other half looked very surprised. "What's wrong?" Mr. Ali asked. Sara explained what everyone had said. Mr. Ali laughed. "This is a perfect lesson," he said. "Today, there is no test. Today, we are going to learn reported speech!"

2Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

1
Why didn't Mr. Ali come on Wednesday?He was sick.
2
Who came instead?A new teacher, Ms. Nadia.
3
What did she say about the test?She said that there would be a short test on Sunday.
4
What did she say it would be about?The stories from Units 1 and 2.
5
What did she tell the students to bring?A pencil.
6
Who did Adam call?Omar, who had been absent.
7
What did Omar tell Huda?That the test was on Sunday, about Unit 2.
8
Where did Huda send a message?To the class group.
9
What did someone write?That there was no test.
10
What did some students say on Saturday night?That the test had been canceled.
11
How many students had pencils on Sunday?Half of them.
12
What did Mr. Ali say they were going to learn?Reported speech!

3Point of view Now Sara gives the exact words that people said.

S

On Wednesday, Ms. Nadia said, "There will be a short test on Sunday. It is about the stories from Units 1 and 2. Bring a pencil, please."

After class, Adam told Omar, "The test is on Sunday. It's about Units 1 and 2." And Omar told Huda, "Adam says the test is on Sunday, about Unit 2."

Huda wrote in our group, "Omar says there's a test on Sunday about Unit 2, or maybe Monday?" Then someone wrote, "There's no test!" And others wrote, "The test has been canceled!"

On Sunday, Mr. Ali laughed. "Today, there is no test. Today, we are going to learn reported speech!"

4What did you learn?

You learned reported speech.

We use it to tell other people what someone said. The verb usually moves one step back into the past.

What she saidWhat we report
"There will be a test."She said that there would be a test.
"The test is on Sunday."He said that the test was on Sunday.
"The test has been canceled."They said that the test had been canceled.
"Bring a pencil."She told us to bring a pencil.
One step back: is → was · will → wouldhas been → had been, can → could
said … or told + a personShe said that… · She told us that…
Orders: told … toShe told us to bring a pencil.
QuestionsWhat did the teacher say?She said that the test would be on Sunday.

5New words

insteadin the place of someone or something
heardthe past of hear
truecorrect; real
canceledstopped; it will not happen
halfone of two equal parts
explainedsaid how or why something happened

Passing On a Message

Telling people what was said in a meeting

Report what someone saidReport questions and ordersCheck that news is true

1Read the conversation

Omar has had a meeting with Mr. Kamal. Back at the new shop, a worker asks him about it.
WWORKERHow was the meeting, Omar? What did Mr. Kamal say?
OOMARHe said that the shop had done very well this month.
WWORKERGreat! Did he say anything about the new screens?
OOMARYes. He said that they would arrive on Thursday.
WWORKERAnd did he ask about the broken laptop?
OOMARHe asked if we had fixed it yet. I told him we were waiting for a part.
WWORKERWhat else did he say?
OOMARHe told us to be extra careful with customers' data. And he said that everyone would get a bonus!
WWORKERA bonus? Did he really say that?
OOMARHe did! He said that we had all worked very hard.

2Useful phrases

Ask about a meeting

What did Mr. Kamal say?

Report news

He said that the shop had done very well.

Report the future

He said that they would arrive on Thursday.

Report a question

He asked if we had fixed it yet.

Report an order

He told us to be extra careful.

Check

Did he really say that?
— He did!

3New words

meetinga time when people meet to talk about work
partone piece of a machine
extramore than usual

bonusextra money for good work

Story · Lesson 9

It Must Be a Ghost!

Strange sounds in Omar's shop late at night. Read the story, then read it from Adam's point of view.

Guess what something isSay how sure you areUse mustmight and can't

1The story

It is late on Thursday night. Omar has closed the new shop, and he is walking home when he remembers his keys. He goes back. Inside, the shop is dark and quiet. Then he hears it, a strange, high sound. Beep… beep… beep. It is coming from the back room.

Omar's heart starts to beat fast. He calls Adam. "There's someone in the shop!" "It can't be a person," Adam says. "You locked the door, didn't you?" "Yes, I did." "Then it might be a cat. Cats sometimes come in through windows." "Cats don't go beep," says Omar. "It must be something electronic."

Adam arrives ten minutes later with a flashlight. They stand at the door of the back room. The sound stops. Then it starts again, louder. "Maybe it's a ghost," Adam whispers. "It can't be a ghost," Omar whispers back, but his voice is shaking. "It could be the alarm. Or it might be one of the phones on the shelf."

Omar opens the door slowly and turns on the light. On the shelf, there are twenty phones waiting for repair. One of them is shining and beeping. Omar picks it up. The screen says, "11:00 p.m. Time to take your medicine, Grandma!" The two friends look at each other and laugh so hard they can't stand up. "It must be Mrs. Fatima's phone," says Omar. "She brought it in yesterday. I'll call her tomorrow and remind her!"

2Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

1
When does Omar go back to the shop?Late on Thursday night.
2
Why does he go back?He remembers his keys.
3
What does he hear?A strange, high sound: beep, beep, beep.
4
Why can't it be a person?Because Omar locked the door.
5
What does Adam think it might be?A cat.
6
Why can't it be a cat?Cats don't go beep.
7
What does Adam bring?A flashlight.
8
What does Adam whisper?Maybe it's a ghost.
9
What does Omar think it could be?The alarm, or one of the phones on the shelf.
10
How many phones are on the shelf?Twenty.
11
What does the phone's screen say?Time to take your medicine, Grandma!
12
Whose phone must it be?Mrs. Fatima's.

3Point of view Now Adam tells it, and how he guessed.

A

It's late on Thursday, and Omar calls me. He's scared. "There's someone in the shop!" It can't be a person, I think. He locked the door. It might be a cat. But cats don't go beep. So it must be something electronic.

I get my flashlight and go to the shop. We stand at the door of the back room. The beeping stops, then it starts again, louder. "Maybe it's a ghost," I whisper. "It can't be a ghost," Omar says, but his voice is shaking. "It could be the alarm."

Omar opens the door and turns on the light. One of the phones on the shelf is beeping. The screen says, "Time to take your medicine, Grandma!"

We laugh so hard we can't stand up. It must be Mrs. Fatima's phone. Some ghost!

4What did you learn?

You learned must, might and can't for guessing.

We use them when we are not completely sure, to show how sure we are.

How sure?Example
Almost sure: yesIt must be something electronic.
MaybeIt might be a cat. · It could be the alarm.
Almost sure: noIt can't be a person. The door is locked.
modal + be or another verbIt must be. She might know.
must for yes, can't for noNot: it mustn't be a person.
might · could mean maybeIt might be a cat. It could be the alarm.
QuestionsWhose phone is it?It must be Mrs. Fatima's.

5New words

beepa short high sound from a machine
electronicworking with electricity and computer parts
ghostthe spirit of a dead person that some people believe in
whispersspeaks very quietly
shakingmoving quickly from side to side
remindhelp someone remember

Science · Lesson 10

Is There Life on Mars?

What scientists know about the red planet, and what they think is possible.

Explain what scientists knowSay what is possible with might and couldUse can't for what is almost impossible

1Read

For hundreds of years, people have looked at the red planet in the night sky and asked the same question. Is there life on Mars?

Mars is the fourth planet from the sun. It is much colder than the Earth, about minus sixty degrees on most days, and its air is very thin. Today, there is no liquid water on its surface. So life there can't be easy.

But scientists have found some exciting clues. Robots called rovers, like Curiosity and Perseverance, have been exploring Mars for years. They have found dry riverbeds and rocks that formed in water. This means that Mars had rivers and lakes billions of years ago.

Where there was water, there could also be life, very small living things called microbes. They might still live deep under the ground, where it is warmer and there could be ice.

Perseverance has been collecting rock samples since 2021. In the future, these samples could come back to Earth, where scientists can study them in labs. If they found even one tiny microbe, it would be one of the biggest discoveries in history.

2Mars in numbers

4thplanet from the sun
−60°on most days
no wateron the surface, today
roversexploring since 2012
Did you know?

A day on Mars is only about 40 minutes longer than a day on Earth, but a year on Mars is 687 Earth days.

3Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

1
Which planet from the sun is Mars?The fourth.
2
Is Mars colder or warmer than the Earth?Much colder, about minus sixty degrees on most days.
3
Is there liquid water on Mars today?No, there isn't.
4
What have the rovers found?Dry riverbeds and rocks that formed in water.
5
What does this mean?Mars had rivers and lakes billions of years ago.
6
Where might microbes still live?Deep under the ground.
7
What has Perseverance been doing since 2021?Collecting rock samples.
8
What would happen if scientists found one tiny microbe?It would be one of the biggest discoveries in history.

4New words

planeta large round object that goes around a sun
surfacethe outside or top of something
exploringtraveling around a place to learn about it
microbesliving things too small to see
samplessmall pieces that are taken to study
discoveriesthings that are found for the first time

Whose Bag Is This?

Guessing who something belongs to

Ask who something belongs toGuess with mustmight and can'tUse clues

1Read the conversation

After class, Mr. Ali finds a bag under a desk. Sara and Huda are still in the room.
MAMR. ALISomeone has left a bag under this desk. Whose is it?
SSARAIt can't be mine. My bag is here.
HHUDAIs there a name on it?
MAMR. ALINo name. But there's a football in it, and a book about planes.
SSARAA book about planes? It must be Adam's!
HHUDABut Omar plays football, too. It might be his.
MAMR. ALIThere's also a phone charger and a receipt from a phone shop.
SSARAHmm. That could be Omar's. He works at a phone shop.
HHUDAWait, there's a sandwich in paper. It says, "For Adam. Love, Mom."
SSARAThen it must be Adam's. Mystery solved!

INTERMEDIATE 2Unit 5 · Lesson 12
Story · Lesson 12

Sara Learns to Drive

Sara decides to learn to drive, and her father offers to teach her. Read the story, then read it from her father's point of view.

Talk about learning something newUse -ing and to after verbsTell how you kept trying

1The story

Sara has always enjoyed solving problems, but there was one problem she couldn't solve. She couldn't drive. Her university is far from her home, and she was tired of waiting for buses. So last month, she decided to learn.

Her father, an engineer, offered to teach her. "Driving is like engineering," he said. "You need to think before you act." On the first day, Sara forgot to look in the mirror. On the second day, she forgot to use the brake! Her father stopped smiling for a moment.

Sara didn't give up. She kept practicing every Friday morning, when the streets were quiet. She practiced parking behind the house, between two old chairs, and she watched videos about changing gears. Slowly, she stopped feeling nervous, and she started to enjoy it.

Last week, Sara passed her driving test on the first try. "I want to thank my teacher," she said, and she hugged her father. That evening, she offered to drive the whole family to the river. Lina was excited, and her mother was a little nervous. And her father? He pretended to read a newspaper in the back seat, but he couldn't stop smiling.

3Point of view Now Sara's father tells it.

F

My daughter Sara has always enjoyed solving problems. Last month, she decided to learn to drive, and I offered to teach her. "You need to think before you act," I told her.

On the first day, she forgot to look in the mirror. On the second day, she forgot to use the brake! I stopped smiling for a moment, I must say.

But she kept practicing every Friday. She practiced parking between two old chairs behind the house, and she watched videos about changing gears. Slowly, she stopped feeling nervous and started to enjoy it.

Last week, she passed her test on the first try. That evening, she drove us all to the river. I pretended to read a newspaper in the back seat, but I couldn't stop smiling.

4What did you learn?

You learned verb + -ing and verb + to.

After some verbs we use the -ing form. After others we use to + verb. Learn each verb with its partner.

INTERMEDIATE 2Unit 5 · Lesson 13
Science · Lesson 13

Gum Arabic

The tree from Sudan that is in your sweets, your drinks, and your medicine.

Explain how a product is madeUse -ing forms as subjectsTalk about Sudan's place in the world

1Read

Have you ever eaten a sweet, had a soft drink, or taken a pill? Then you have probably used something from Sudan, gum arabic.

Gum arabic is a natural gum from the acacia tree, which grows across the dry lands of Africa. Sudan is the biggest producer in the world. In some years, it has produced more than half of all the gum arabic on Earth, mostly from the Kordofan and Darfur regions.

Collecting the gum is slow work. In the dry season, farmers make small cuts in the bark of the trees. This is called tapping. Over the next weeks, a thick liquid comes out of the cuts and slowly becomes hard in the sun. Then the farmers start picking the hard pieces, which look like small yellow stones, by hand.

The gum is sold to companies all over the world. It is used to keep drinks mixed, to make sweets soft, to cover pills, and even to make ink and paint.

The acacia tree also helps the land. Its roots stop the sand from moving, and it can grow where other trees can't. So planting acacia trees is good for farmers and for the environment.

2From tree to world

1tappingfarmers cut the bark
2dryingthe gum becomes hard
3pickingpieces are picked by hand
4sellingsent all over the world
Did you know?

The "gum arabic belt" is a long line of acacia trees across Africa, south of the Sahara, from Senegal in the west to Sudan in the east.
